summary: When a mother animal is shechted, her unborn calf may be eaten too. But if the calf's head already came out, it counts as born and needs its own shechitah.

chunks.st: and then the mother animal was slaughtered, the consumption of the fetus is permitted
chunks.stMore: by virtue of the slaughter of the mother animal.

chunks.en: If it put out its head,
chunks.st: But if the fetus extended its head outside the womb,

stIntro: When a pregnant kosher animal is slaughtered, the slaughter also renders the consumption of its fetus permitted.

summary: A baby bechor (firstborn animal) is holy once it is born. If the mother had trouble giving birth and he had to cut up the calf before it was born, it is not holy; if most of it came out, it must be buried.

chunks.en: An animal having her first calf, with a hard birth:
chunks.st: If an animal that was giving birth to a firstborn male was encountering difficulty giving birth, and in order to alleviate the difficulty one wishes to terminate the birth,

chunks.en: he may cut it up piece by piece and throw it to the dogs.
chunks.explain: Because it was not born yet, it is not holy.
chunks.st: he may cut up the fetus limb by limb and cast it to the dogs. Since the fetus was not born, it is non-sacred and does not require burial.

chunks.en: If most of it came out,
chunks.st: If a majority of the fetus had already emerged, it is considered to have been born and is therefore consecrated; consequently, if one cut it up

chunks.en: it must be buried,
chunks.st: it must be buried, and the mother animal is

chunks.en: and the mother is free from the bechor rule.
chunks.explain: Her later calves will not be holy as a bechor.
chunks.st: exempted from having firstborn status conferred on any future offspring.

stIntro: Upon its birth, the firstborn male offspring of a domesticated animal is automatically consecrated with firstborn status, and it is prohibited to derive benefit from it. Furthermore, if it dies, it may not be discarded, but must be buried.

summary: If an unborn animal died inside its mother and the shepherd touched it, he stays tahor. But if a woman's unborn baby died and the midwife touched it, the midwife becomes tamei for seven days.

chunks.he: בְּהֵמָה שֶׁמֵּת עֻבָּרָהּ בְּתוֹךְ מֵעֶיהָ וְהוֹשִׁיט
chunks.en: An animal whose unborn calf died inside her, and the shepherd reached in
chunks.st: With regard to an animal whose fetus died in its womb and

chunks.en: his hand and touched it,
chunks.st: the shepherd reached his hand into the womb and touched the fetus,

chunks.en: whether in a non-kosher animal,
chunks.st: both in the case of a non-kosher animal

chunks.en: or in a kosher animal,
chunks.st: and in the case of a kosher animal the fetus does not have the status of an animal carcass that imparts ritual impurity, and the shepherd remains

chunks.en: he is tahor. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says:
chunks.st: ritually pure. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says:

chunks.en: In a non-kosher animal, he is tamei,
chunks.st: In the case of a non-kosher animal it is impure,

chunks.en: and in a kosher animal, he is tahor.
chunks.st: and in the case of a kosher animal it is pure.

chunks.he: הָאִשָּׁה שֶׁמֵּת וְלָדָהּ בְּתוֹךְ מֵעֶיהָ וּפָשְׁטָה
chunks.en: A woman whose unborn baby died inside her, and the midwife
chunks.st: With regard to a woman whose fetus died in her womb and the

chunks.en: reached in her hand and touched it:
chunks.st: midwife extended her hand into the womb and touched the fetus,

chunks.en: the midwife becomes tamei for seven days,
chunks.st: the midwife is thereby rendered impure with the seven-day impurity imparted by a corpse,

chunks.en: and the woman stays tahor until the baby comes out.
chunks.st: and the woman remains ritually pure until the offspring emerges from the womb.

summary: If an unborn calf's leg came out and was cut off after the mother was shechted, Rabbi Meir says the meat touched a neveilah, and the Sages disagree. The mishnah then shows how we know that shechting a treifah keeps it from being a tamei neveilah.

chunks.en: An animal having a hard time giving birth,
chunks.st: If an animal was encountering difficulty giving birth

chunks.en: and the unborn calf put out its front leg, and he cut it off,
chunks.st: and as a result the fetus extended its foreleg outside the mother’s womb, and someone severed it

chunks.en: and afterwards he shechted its mother:
chunks.st: and afterward slaughtered the mother animal,

chunks.en: the meat is tahor.
chunks.st: the flesh of the fetus is ritually pure.

chunks.he: שָׁחַט אֶת אִמּוֹ וְאַחַר כָּךְ חֲתָכָהּ,
chunks.en: If he shechted its mother and afterwards cut off the leg,
chunks.st: If one first slaughtered the mother animal and afterward severed the foreleg,

chunks.en: the meat has touched a neveilah.
chunks.explain: The cut-off leg counts as a neveilah.
chunks.st: the flesh of both the mother animal and the fetus are ritually impure due to having been in contact with a carcass.
chunks.stMore: Since the foreleg was not permitted to be consumed through the act of slaughtering, it is regarded as a carcass with the associated ritual impurity. The rest of the flesh, which was permitted to be consumed by the slaughter, was in contact with it and so was rendered ritually impure from it;

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Meir says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: And the Sages say:
chunks.st: And the Rabbis say: The flesh has the ritual impurity of having been in

chunks.en: It touched a treifah that was shechted.
chunks.explain: That is a lighter kind of tumah.
chunks.st: contact with a tereifa that was slaughtered,
chunks.stMore: as the limb is regarded as a tereifa that was slaughtered. By Torah law, although it is prohibited to consume it, it does not impart ritual impurity. Nevertheless, the Sages decreed that a tereifa that was slaughtered, as well as anything that comes in contact with it, is regarded as ritually impure to the extent that it disqualifies sacrificial foods that come in contact with it.

chunks.en: Just as we find that a treifah's shechitah makes it tahor,
chunks.st: The Rabbis explain the rationale behind their opinion: Just as we found in the case of a tereifa that its slaughter renders it ritually pure according to Torah law,
chunks.stMore: i.e., ritual slaughter prevents it from having the ritual impurity of a carcass despite not rendering the animal permitted for consumption,

chunks.he: אַף שְׁחִיטַת בְּהֵמָה תְּטַהֵר אֶת הָאֵבָר.
chunks.en: so too the shechitah of the mother should make the leg tahor.
chunks.st: so too, the slaughter of the mother animal should render the limb of its fetus that left the womb ritually pure,
chunks.stMore: despite the fact that its consumption is prohibited.

chunks.en: Rabbi Meir said to them:
chunks.st: Rabbi Meir said to them:

chunks.he: לֹא, אִם טִהֲרָה שְׁחִיטַת טְרֵפָה אוֹתָהּ,
chunks.en: No! If a treifah's shechitah makes it tahor,
chunks.st: No, if the slaughter of a tereifa renders the body of the animal ritually pure,

chunks.en: that is something that is part of its body.
chunks.st: it is because the slaughter is performed on something that is part of its body, i.e., its throat.

chunks.en: Should it make the leg tahor,
chunks.st: Does it necessarily follow that you should also render the limb that left the womb pure,

chunks.en: something that is not part of its body?
chunks.st: given that it is something that is not part of the mother’s body? Certainly not.

chunks.en: How do we know that a treifah's shechitah makes it tahor?
chunks.st: The mishna asks: From where is it derived with regard to a tereifa that its slaughter renders it ritually pure, i.e., prevents it from having the ritual impurity of a carcass?
chunks.stMore: The mishna notes there is a reason to say the slaughter should not render it pure, as one can compare a tereifa with a non-kosher animal:

chunks.en: A non-kosher animal may not be eaten,
chunks.st: A non-kosher animal is prohibited for consumption;

chunks.en: and a treifah may not be eaten.
chunks.st: so too, a tereifa is prohibited for consumption.

chunks.he: מַה בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה אֵין שְׁחִיטָתָהּ מְטַהַרְתָּהּ,
chunks.en: Just as a non-kosher animal's shechitah does not make it tahor,
chunks.st: Therefore, conclude: Just as with regard to a non-kosher animal, its slaughter does not render it ritually pure,

chunks.en: so too a treifah's shechitah should not make it tahor!
chunks.st: so too with regard to a tereifa, its slaughter should not render it ritually pure.

chunks.he: לֹא, אִם אָמַרְתָּ בִּבְהֵמָה טְמֵאָה שֶׁלֹּא
chunks.en: No! If you said this about a non-kosher animal, which never
chunks.st: The mishna questions the comparison: No, if you said that slaughtering cannot prevent an animal from having the ritual impurity of a carcass in the case of a non-kosher animal,

chunks.en: had a time when it could be kosher,
chunks.st: which is distinct in that it did not have a period of potential fitness
chunks.stMore: when slaughtering it could have rendered its consumption permitted,

chunks.he: תֹּאמַר בִּטְרֵפָה שֶׁהָיְתָה לָהּ שְׁעַת הַכֹּשֶׁר.
chunks.en: should you say it about a treifah, which did have a time when it could be kosher?
chunks.st: does it necessarily follow that you should also say this in the case of a tereifa, which did have a period of potential fitness?
chunks.stMore: Perhaps, since the animal had a period of potential fitness its slaughter remains effective in preventing it from having the ritual impurity of a carcass.

chunks.en: Take back what you brought!
chunks.st: The mishna rejects this distinction: Take back to yourself this claim that you brought,
chunks.stMore: as it is insufficient.

chunks.he: הֲרֵי שֶׁנּוֹלְדָה טְרֵפָה מִן הַבֶּטֶן מִנַּיִן.
chunks.en: What about one born a treifah from the womb? How do we know?
chunks.st: What about a case where an animal was born as a tereifa from the womb, and so it never had a period of potential fitness? For such a case, from where is it derived that its slaughter renders it ritually pure?

chunks.en: No! If you said this about a non-kosher animal,
chunks.st: The mishna reformulates the distinction: No, if you say that slaughtering cannot prevent a prohibited animal from having the ritual impurity of a carcass with regard to a non-kosher animal,

chunks.en: whose kind never has shechitah,
chunks.st: which is distinct in that there are no animals of its kind that are permitted through slaughtering,
chunks.stMore: as the Torah states the concept of slaughtering only with regard to kosher animals,

chunks.en: should you say it about a treifah, whose kind does have shechitah?
chunks.st: does it necessarily follow that you should also say this with regard to a tereifa kosher animal, given that there are other animals of its kind that are permitted through slaughtering, i.e., kosher animals that are not tereifa?
chunks.stMore: Perhaps, since the concept of slaughtering is relevant to that kind of animal it can serve to prevent the animal from having the ritual impurity of a carcass even if the slaughter cannot render it permitted for consumption. The mishna notes: Based on this reasoning, one must conclude that with regard to

chunks.en: A baby animal born alive after eight months,
chunks.st: an eight-month-old fetus that was born alive,

chunks.en: its shechitah does not make it tahor,
chunks.st: slaughter does not render it ritually pure,

chunks.en: because its kind has no shechitah.
chunks.st: as there are no animals of its kind that are permitted through slaughtering.
chunks.stMore: The Torah applies the concept of slaughter only with regard to animals that were born full term.

summary: An unborn calf found inside a shechted animal may be eaten because of its mother's shechitah. If it is a full-term live calf, Rabbi Meir says it needs its own shechitah, but the Sages say its mother's shechitah is enough.

chunks.en: Someone who shechted an animal and found in it
chunks.st: In the case of one who slaughtered an animal and found within it an

chunks.en: an eight-month calf, alive or dead,
chunks.explain: Eight months is too early to be fully grown.
chunks.st: eight-month-old fetus, i.e., one that was not full term, whether it was alive or dead,

chunks.en: or a nine-month calf that is dead,
chunks.st: or a nine-month-old fetus, i.e., one that was full term, that was dead,
chunks.stMore: that fetus is permitted by virtue of the slaughter of its mother, as it is considered part of its mother. Therefore, its blood is considered part of its mother’s blood and is prohibited, so one must

chunks.en: he tears it open and takes out its blood.
chunks.st: tear the fetus and remove its blood before it may be consumed.

chunks.en: If he found a nine-month calf alive,
chunks.st: If he found within it a live nine-month-old fetus,

chunks.en: it needs shechitah,
chunks.st: it requires its own slaughter, as it is considered an independent full-fledged animal,

chunks.en: and he is liable for "it and its child".
chunks.explain: The Torah forbids shechting a mother and its child on the same day.
chunks.st: and if one slaughters both the mother and fetus on the same day, one is liable for violating the prohibition against slaughtering an animal itself and its offspring on the same day;

chunks.en: That is what Rabbi Meir says.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Rabbi Meir.

chunks.en: And the Sages say:
chunks.st: And the Rabbis say:
chunks.stMore: Even when the fetus is nine months old, it is still considered part of its mother, and

chunks.en: Its mother's shechitah makes it allowed.
chunks.st: the slaughter of its mother renders it permitted for consumption.

chunks.en: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says:
chunks.st: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says:

chunks.he: אֲפִלּוּ בֶן שְׁמֹנֶה שָׁנִים וְחוֹרֵשׁ בַּשָּׂדֶה,
chunks.en: Even if it grew up for years and is plowing in the field,
chunks.st: Even if the fetus emerged alive and is now five years old and plowing in the field,

chunks.en: its mother's shechitah made it allowed.
chunks.st: the earlier slaughter of its mother rendered it permitted and it does not require slaughter before it is eaten.

chunks.he: קְרָעָהּ וּמָצָא בָהּ בֶּן תִּשְׁעָה חַי,
chunks.en: If he tore the mother open and found in her a live nine-month calf,
chunks.st: But if one tore an animal, i.e., he killed it without slaughtering it, and inside he found a live nine-month-old fetus, everyone agrees that the fetus

chunks.en: it needs shechitah,
chunks.st: requires its own slaughter

chunks.en: because its mother was not shechted.
chunks.st: because its mother was not slaughtered.

summary: If an animal's legs were cut off below the knee joint it is kosher, but above it, it is a treifah. If a bone broke but most of the meat around it is whole, shechitah makes that leg allowed.

chunks.he: בְּהֵמָה שֶׁנֶּחְתְּכוּ רַגְלֶיהָ מִן הָאַרְכֻּבָּה וּלְמַטָּה,
chunks.en: An animal whose legs were cut off from the knee joint and down
chunks.st: With regard to an animal whose hind legs were severed, if they were severed from the leg joint and below, the animal is

chunks.en: is kosher. From the knee joint and up,
chunks.st: kosher; from the leg joint and above, the animal is thereby rendered a tereifa and is

chunks.en: it is pasul. And also one whose meeting of the sinews was taken out.
chunks.st: not kosher. And likewise, an animal whose convergence of sinews in the thigh was removed is a tereifa and is not kosher.

chunks.en: If the bone broke,
chunks.st: If the bone of a limb was broken but the limb was not completely severed, and the animal was then slaughtered,

chunks.en: if most of the meat around it is still whole,
chunks.st: if the majority of the flesh surrounding the bone is intact,

chunks.en: its shechitah makes it allowed.
chunks.st: the slaughter of the animal renders it permitted;

chunks.en: But if not,
chunks.st: but if not,

chunks.en: its shechitah does not make it allowed.
chunks.st: its slaughter does not render it permitted.

summary: The afterbirth found inside a shechted animal may be eaten by someone who does not mind, and it is not counted as food for tumah unless he plans to eat it. The mishnah also forbids burying or hanging it in superstitious ways.

chunks.he: הַשּׁוֹחֵט אֶת הַבְּהֵמָה וּמָצָא בָהּ שִׁלְיָא,
chunks.en: Someone who shechts an animal and finds the afterbirth inside it:
chunks.explain: The afterbirth is the sac that a baby animal grows in.
chunks.st: In the case of one who slaughters an animal and finds a placenta in its womb, one with

chunks.en: someone who is not disgusted may eat it.
chunks.st: a hearty soul [nefesh hayafa], i.e., who is not repulsed by it, may eat it,
chunks.stMore: as its consumption was permitted by virtue of the slaughter of the mother. Nevertheless, since generally speaking, people do not consume such placentas, it is not regarded as food

words.note: Someone who is not picky or disgusted.

chunks.en: And it does not become tamei with the tumah
chunks.st: and so it cannot become impure with

chunks.en: of food, nor with the tumah of a neveilah.
chunks.st: the ritual impurity of food even were it to come into contact with a source of impurity. And furthermore, it does not impart the ritual impurity of animal carcasses
chunks.stMore: as it was permitted by virtue of the slaughter of the mother.

chunks.en: If he planned to eat it,
chunks.st: But if one intended to eat it, one thereby elevated it to the status of food, and the placenta

chunks.en: it can get the tumah of food, but
chunks.st: becomes impure with the ritual impurity of food
chunks.stMore: if it comes into contact with a source of impurity.

chunks.en: not the tumah of a neveilah.
chunks.st: But even so, it still does not impart the ritual impurity of animal carcasses.

chunks.en: An afterbirth that partly came out
chunks.st: With regard to a placenta, part of which emerged from the womb before the mother was slaughtered,

chunks.en: may not be eaten.
chunks.st: its consumption is prohibited even after the mother animal is slaughtered because the emergence of the placenta is

chunks.en: It is a sign of a baby in a woman,
chunks.st: an indication of a fetus in a woman

chunks.en: and a sign of a baby in an animal.
chunks.st: and an indication of a fetus in an animal.
chunks.stMore: Accordingly, there is a concern that the head of the fetus might have emerged in that part of the placenta, thereby rendering the fetus as having been born, a status that precludes it from being permitted by the slaughter of its mother. Since the offspring is prohibited, its placenta is likewise prohibited.

chunks.en: An animal having her first that lost an afterbirth:
chunks.st: If an animal that was giving birth to its firstborn expelled a placenta,

chunks.en: he may throw it to the dogs.
chunks.st: one may cast it to the dogs,
chunks.stMore: and one does not need to be concerned that the placenta came from a male fetus that has the consecrated status of a firstborn.

chunks.en: But with korban animals, it must be buried.
chunks.st: But in the case of sacrificial animals the placenta must be buried,
chunks.stMore: because it came from a fetus that is assumed to have been sacred. The mishna adds:

chunks.en: But we may not bury it at a crossroads,
chunks.st: But one may neither bury it at an intersection,

chunks.en: and we may not hang it on a tree,
chunks.st: nor may one hang it on a tree, superstitious rites intended to prevent the animal from miscarrying again,

chunks.en: because of the ways of the Emori.
chunks.st: due to the prohibition against following the ways of the Amorite,
chunks.stMore: which prohibits Jews from practicing the superstitious rites observed by gentiles.
